check.q: Take the digit cards 4, 0 and 9. Make the biggest 3-digit number you can. Move the cards around to try.
check.why: Biggest digit first, then the next biggest: 9, 4, 0.

check.q: Now use the cards 4, 0, 9 and 3, each once. What is the smallest ODD 4-digit number? Say how you know.
check.why: Odd means the ones digit is 9 or 3. 0 cannot go first. Try 3049 and 4093: 3049 is smaller.

inv.title: What if one card changes?
inv.intro: The cards 1, 2, 3, 4 make 24 four-digit numbers: 6 start with each card. Now change the 4 card to a 0, so the cards are 0, 1, 2, 3.
parts: Make a list in order of the numbers that start with 1. How many are there?
How many start with 2? With 3? With 0?
How many 4-digit numbers can you make altogether now? What stayed the same? What changed? Why?
inv.model: Starting with 1: 1023, 1032, 1203, 1230, 1302, 1320 (6 numbers). 6 start with 2 and 6 start with 3. None start with 0 (0123 is only a 3-digit number). Altogether 18, not 24. Same: each of the cards 1, 2, 3 still makes 6 numbers. Changed: 0 cannot go first, so 6 numbers are lost (24 − 6 = 18). Look for: a list in order, a count by first digit, and the reason that zero cannot lead. Extension: how many are even? (10 with the cards 0, 1, 2, 3; 12 with the cards 1, 2, 3, 4.)
inv.easy: Easy first step: with the cards 0, 1, 2, 3, write only the numbers that start with 1. Use the cards to help you.

1.go: Cards 2, 4, 5, 8 now: how many numbers between 4000 and 6000? Which is closest to 5000?
1.goans: 12 numbers: 6 start with 4 and 6 start with 5 (2, 4, 5, 8 each once). Closest to 5000: 4852 (148 away); the nearest above is 5248.

check.q: Find the missing digit A:  2A5 + 134 = 389. Try each digit for A, or add the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds.
check.why: Tens: A + 3 must make 8, so A = 5. Check: 255 + 134 = 389.

check.q: Ali had some marbles. He won 1250 more and then had 4000. How many did he have at first? Draw a number line if it helps.
check.why: Work backwards: take away what he won. 4000 − 1250 = 2750. Check: 2750 + 1250 = 4000.

inv.title: Is it always true? The reverse trick
inv.intro: Take a 3-digit number whose first digit is bigger than its last digit, like 842. Reverse it to make 248. Subtract the smaller from the bigger: 842 − 248 = 594.
parts: Try 4 more numbers of your own. Write each subtraction and its answer.
What do you notice about all your answers? Compare with a partner.
Is it always true? Test it on a number that ends in 0, like 720, then explain why you think it works.
inv.model: Every answer is in the 99 times table: 99 × (first digit − last digit). 842 − 248 = 594 = 99 × 6 (8 − 2 = 6); 720 − 27 = 693 = 99 × 7. This is true for every 3-digit number whose first digit is bigger than its last (checked by computer for all of them). Why: the middle digit is in the same place in both numbers, so it cancels. The hundreds and ones swap places, so each step of difference between the first and last digits adds 99 (100 − 1). Look for: several tests, spotting the 99s (not only 495; 495 appears only when the digits differ by 5), and any reason about the middle digit. Extension: when is the answer exactly 495?
inv.easy: Easy first step: try 842 − 248 = 594 for yourself. Then try 953 and 351 (reverse it, then subtract).

2.go: With the cards 1 to 9, what is the smallest answer you can make? The biggest?
2.goans: Smallest 459 (for example 173 + 286); biggest 981 (for example 235 + 746). Every answer has digits adding to 18.

check.q: Here is the 7 times table: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56, 63, 70. Which of these numbers are in it: 49, 54, 63?
check.why: Look along the table: 49 and 63 are there; 54 is not.

check.q: You know 6 × 7 = 42. Use it to work out 6 × 14 and 6 × 6. Say how you did it.
check.why: 14 is double 7, so double 42 = 84. 6 × 6 is one 6 less than 6 × 7: 42 − 6 = 36.

inv.title: Is it always true? Digit sums
inv.intro: In the 9 times table the digits of each answer add up to 9: 9, 18 (1 + 8), 27 (2 + 7), 36 (3 + 6) ...
parts: Carry on the 9 times table to 9 × 12. Add the digits of each answer. Is the total ALWAYS 9? Write what you find.
Try the 3 times table and the 6 times table up to × 12. Add the digits of each answer. What do you notice?
Try the 4 times table. Is it the same? What can you say about the 3, 6 and 9 times tables?
inv.model: 9 times table: the digit sum is 9 for 9 × 1 to 9 × 10 and for 9 × 12 = 108, but 9 × 11 = 99 gives 9 + 9 = 18. So 'always 9' is false, but 18 is also in the 9 times table (and 1 + 8 = 9 again). 3 and 6 times tables: every digit sum is in the 3 times table (3, 6, 9, 12, ...). 4 times table: digit sums 4, 8, 3, 7, 2, 6, 10 ... include numbers that are not in the 3 times table (4, 8), so it is not the same. Conclusion: the digit sum of any answer in the 3, 6 or 9 table is in the 3 times table; for the 9 table it is in the 9 times table. Look for: testing past × 10, finding the counterexample 99, and revising the claim instead of just saying 'no'. Do not expect a proof.
inv.easy: Easy first step: write the 9 times table up to 9 × 6 and add the digits of each answer.

3.go: Try the 5s and the 9s. How many dots does each table touch? Why?
3.goans: The 5s touch only 2 dots (5 and 0). The 9s touch all 10 dots, going round the other way, like the 1s, because each 9 times answer is 1 less in the ones place than the one before.

check.q: Ali has 70 stickers and Ben has 30. Draw two bars, or use counters. How many stickers must Ali give Ben so that they have the same number?
check.why: The difference is 40. Ali gives half of it: 20. Then both have 50.

check.q: Ali has $12. Ben has $5 less than Ali. Mei has twice as much as Ben. How much money does Mei have? Draw bars to help.
check.why: Ben has 12 − 5 = $7. Mei has two bars the same as Ben's: 7 + 7 = $14.

inv.title: What stays the same?
inv.intro: Mei is 13 years old and her brother is 5.
parts: Fill in the table for the next 5 years.
What stays the same every year? What changes? How does it change?
Will Mei ever be exactly DOUBLE her brother's age? When? What about TRIPLE? Explain.
inv.model: Table (Mei, brother, difference, total): now 13, 5, 8, 18; 1: 14, 6, 8, 20; 2: 15, 7, 8, 22; 3: 16, 8, 8, 24; 4: 17, 9, 8, 26; 5: 18, 10, 8, 28. Same: the difference is always 8. Changes: both ages go up by 1 and the total goes up by 2 each year. Double: in 3 years (16 and 8). Mei is double when her brother's age equals the difference, 8. Triple: never again. She was triple last year (12 and 4), and after that the ratio only gets smaller. Look for: using the table, noticing the difference is constant, and a bar-model reason for 'double' (her brother's bar is the same length as the difference). Extension: when did she last have 3 times his age?
inv.easy: Easy first step: fill in the first row. In 1 year Mei is 14 and her brother is 6. What is the difference?

4.go: Make 3 towers from 30 cubes, each 2 cubes taller than the last. How tall is each? (Then 3 taller.)
4.goans: 30 cubes: 8, 10, 12 (3 towers, take away 2 + 4 = 6, share 24 into 3). With 3 taller each time: 7, 10, 13 (30 - 9 = 21, 21 / 3 = 7).

check.q: Mei puts 13 sweets in bags of 4. Use counters or draw it. How many full bags can she make? How many sweets are left over?
check.why: 3 bags of 4 use 12 sweets. 1 sweet is left.

check.q: Ali says, "6 sweets are left over when I put the sweets in bags of 6." Draw 6 sweets in bags of 6. What is wrong?
check.a: 6 sweets fill a bag, so 0 are left
check.why: A leftover must be fewer than 6, otherwise another bag of 6 can be filled.

inv.title: Is it always true? Three in a row
inv.intro: Write any three whole numbers in a row, like 14, 15, 16. Exactly one of them is in the 3 times table (15).
parts: Try 5 different starting numbers (make one of them bigger than 100). Circle the number in the 3 times table each time. Is it always exactly one?
Explain why. Think about the remainders when you divide by 3.
What if we change it? Try 4 numbers in a row and the 4 times table. Then try only 2 numbers in a row and the 3 times table.
inv.model: Always true: among 3 numbers in a row there is exactly one in the 3 times table. Remainders when dividing by 3 go 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, ... so in any 3 in a row each remainder 0, 1, 2 appears once, and remainder 0 means it is in the table. With 4 in a row and the 4 times table it is also exactly one (remainders 0, 1, 2, 3 repeat). With only 2 in a row and the 3 times table it is NOT always true (4 and 5 have none). In general, n numbers in a row always have exactly one in the n times table. Look for: several tests including a big number, the remainder cycle as the reason, and a counterexample for the 2 in a row case.
inv.easy: Easy first step: circle the number in the 3 times table in 14, 15, 16. Then try 20, 21, 22.

5.go: 49 counters: which group sizes from 2 to 8 leave 1 over? Why?
5.goans: 49 = 48 + 1. Sizes 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 leave 1 over (48 is in all those tables). Size 5 leaves 4 and size 7 leaves 0 (49 = 7 x 7).

check.q: Draw a rectangle. Cut it into 4 equal parts and shade 1 part. What fraction did you shade?
check.why: 4 equal parts, 1 shaded: one quarter.

check.q: Mei says, "1/4 of a pizza is bigger than 1/3 of the same pizza, because 4 is bigger than 3." Is she right? Draw it.
check.why: More equal parts means each part is smaller. Quarters are smaller than thirds.

inv.title: Find all the ways
inv.intro: Make exactly [[3/4]] using pieces of [[1/2]], [[1/4]] and [[1/8]]. You may use as many of each as you like. Order does not matter ([[1/2]] + [[1/4]] is the same way as [[1/4]] + [[1/2]]).
parts: List every way. Start with the most halves.
How do you know you have found them all?
What if we want exactly 1 whole instead? Do you think there will be more ways or fewer? Test your idea.
inv.model: 3/4 is the same as 6/8. The 6 ways (halves, quarters, eighths): 1 half + 1 quarter; 1 half + 2 eighths; 3 quarters; 2 quarters + 2 eighths; 1 quarter + 4 eighths; 6 eighths. Systematic: fix the number of halves (1 or 0), then the quarters, then fill with eighths. For 1 whole there are 9 ways, so more. Look for: a list in order, an organised method for 'all', and a reason that more room means more ways. Using the fraction wall is expected.
inv.easy: Easy first step: make [[3/4]] with one half. How much is left to fill?

6.go: Find 3 DIFFERENT pieces that make exactly [[1/2]]. Is there another way?
6.goans: Only one way with three different pieces: 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12 (3/12 + 2/12 + 1/12 = 6/12). Other ways repeat a piece, e.g. 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8.

check.q: Draw a rectangle 3 cm long and 2 cm wide on squared paper (or use 6 tiles). How many squares does it cover? How far is it all the way round the edge?
check.why: 6 squares cover it. Walk round the edge: 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10.

check.q: Two different rectangles both cover 12 squares. Can the distance all the way round the edge be different? Show two examples.
check.why: 1 by 12 is 26 cm round; 2 by 6 is 16 cm round; 3 by 4 is 14 cm round.

inv.title: What if we change it? What stays the same?
inv.intro: A square with sides 4 cm has area 16 cm² and perimeter 16 cm. Make it 1 cm longer one way and 1 cm shorter the other way. You get a 5 cm by 3 cm rectangle.
parts: Work out the area and perimeter of the 5 by 3 rectangle. What changed? What stayed the same?
Do the same for a 6 cm square (7 by 5) and a 10 cm square (11 by 9). Fill in the table. Then choose a square of your own.
Is it always true? Draw the 4 by 4 square and explain what happens to the area.
inv.model: 4 by 4: perimeter 16, area 16 becomes 5 by 3: perimeter 16, area 15. 6 cm: 24 and 36 become 7 by 5: 24 and 35. 10 cm: 40 and 100 become 11 by 9: 40 and 99. The perimeter stays the same and the area is always exactly 1 cm² smaller. This is true for every square (checked by computer for sides 2 to 499). Why: move the bottom row of 4 squares to the right side. The new column is only 3 squares tall, so 3 squares fit and 1 is left over. Look for: several tests, the pattern 'area drops by 1', and any picture or cut-and-move reason. Extension: what if we make it 2 cm longer and 2 cm shorter? (area drops by 4; perimeter still the same).
inv.easy: Easy first step: work out the area and perimeter of the 4 by 4 square and of the 5 by 3 rectangle.

7.go: 16 squares: make every rectangle. Which has the longest way round the edge? The shortest?
7.goans: 16 squares: 1 by 16 (34 cm round), 2 by 8 (20 cm), 4 by 4 (16 cm). Longest 1 by 16, shortest 4 by 4: the square, the most compact shape.

check.q: Look at the letters L, H and O. Which letters have a square corner? Which letter has two lines that never meet, however far they go?
check.a: L and H have square corners; H has two lines that never meet
check.why: L and H have square corners; O has none. The two upright lines of H stay the same distance apart.

check.q: Draw a rectangle. Draw a straight line from one corner to the opposite corner. You get two triangles. How many right angles does each triangle have? How do you know?
check.why: Only the corner that was not cut is still a right angle. The corners that were cut are split into two smaller angles.

inv.title: Staircase corners: find the pattern
inv.intro: A 1-step staircase is 1 square. A 2-step staircase has 3 squares (a column of 2 beside a column of 1). A 3-step staircase has 6 squares.
parts: Count the corners of each staircase where the inside angle is a right angle. Then count the corners where the inside angle is BIGGER than a right angle. Draw the 4-step staircase and fill in the table.
What pattern do you see? Use it to fill in the 10-step row without drawing.
Is the number of corners always an even number? Why do you think so?

cols: Corners bigger than a right angle

inv.model: Steps 1 to 4: right angles 4, 5, 6, 7; bigger than a right angle 0, 1, 2, 3; all corners 4, 6, 8, 10. So right-angle corners = steps + 3, bigger corners = steps − 1, all corners = 2 × steps + 2. 10 steps: 13, 9 and 22 (checked by computer by building each staircase). The total is always even because each new step adds 2 corners (one right angle and one dent). Look for: careful organised counting, a table, a stated rule, and a prediction that can be checked. Any pair can draw the 10-step staircase to test the prediction.
inv.easy: Easy first step: draw the 1-step and 2-step staircases. Count the corners of the 2-step staircase.

8.go: Fold your corner in half again. Smaller or bigger than a right angle? Find two.
8.goans: Smaller than a right angle: it is half of a right angle, so two of them make one right angle. It appears at the corner of a set square, or when a square is cut along its diagonal.

check.q: Which is longer: 1 m or 90 cm? Say how you know.
check.why: 1 m is 100 cm, and 100 is more than 90.

check.q: A film starts at 3:45 p.m. and lasts 1 hour 30 minutes. When does it end? Say how you counted.
check.why: 3:45 + 1 h = 4:45. 15 minutes more makes 5:00, and 15 more makes 5:15.

inv.title: Find all the ways to pay
inv.intro: Ali pays exactly 50 cents using only 5-cent, 10-cent and 20-cent coins. He can use as many of each coin as he likes.
parts: Find all the ways. Write each way in the table (how many of each coin).
Which way uses the FEWEST coins? Which uses the MOST?
How do you know you have found them all?
inv.model: There are 12 ways (20c, 10c, 5c coins): 2,1,0; 2,0,2; 1,3,0; 1,2,2; 1,1,4; 1,0,6; 0,5,0; 0,4,2; 0,3,4; 0,2,6; 0,1,8; 0,0,10. Fewest coins: two 20c and one 10c (3 coins). Most: ten 5c coins (10 coins). Systematic method: fix the number of 20c coins (2, then 1, then 0), then the number of 10c coins, then fill with 5c coins. Look for: an organised list, no repeats (the same set of coins in a different order is one way), and the reason for being sure. Extension: what if we also have a 50c coin? (13 ways).
inv.easy: Easy first step: pay 50 cents with ten 5-cent coins. Then swap some of them for 10-cent coins.

9.go: 12 friends and $30: how many bottles of punch? Can you spend exactly $30?
9.goans: 12 x 250 ml = 3000 ml = 3 l, so 2 bottles (2 l each) at least. Yes, there are many ways, e.g. 2 punch + 3 cupcakes + 3 balloons ($6 + $16.50 + $7.50), or 2 curry puffs + 2 punch + 2 cupcakes + 2 balloons.

check.q: Ali, Ben and Mei stand in a line. Use three name cards (or write A, B, M). How many different orders can you find?
check.why: ABM, AMB, BAM, BMA, MAB, MBA. Listing by who is first helps to find them all.

check.q: Now Ben must stand somewhere in front of Mei (not always right in front). Which of your orders are still allowed?
check.why: Cross out every order where Mei comes before Ben.

inv.title: Handshakes: draw it, list it, make a table
inv.intro: Some friends meet. Everyone shakes hands with every other friend once. Two friends make 1 handshake.
parts: Find the number of handshakes for 3, 4, 5 and 6 friends. Draw dots and lines, or make a list, to help. Fill in the table.
What pattern do you see? Use it to find the handshakes for 10 friends.
Could there ever be exactly 20 handshakes? Explain.

cols: How many more than the row above?

inv.model: 2 friends: 1; 3: 3; 4: 6; 5: 10; 6: 15. The extra amount goes up by 2, 3, 4, 5, so 7 friends: 21, 8: 28, 9: 36, 10: 45. Reason: each new friend shakes hands with everyone already there. 10 friends: 9 + 8 + 7 + ... + 1 = 45. 20 handshakes is impossible: 6 friends give 15 and 7 friends give 21 (checked by computer for every group size). Look for: a drawing or an organised list, the pattern in the jumps, and a sensible check of the 20 claim using the table. Extension: how many for 20 friends? (190)
inv.easy: Easy first step: draw 3 dots and join every pair. Count the lines. Then try 4 dots.

10.go: A 120 cm ribbon is cut into 4 pieces, each 10 cm longer than the last. How long is each?
10.goans: 15 cm, 25 cm, 35 cm and 45 cm (take away 10 + 20 + 30 = 60, 60 cm left, 60 / 4 = 15).
